title: The Duration That Cannot Be Counted: Bergson from the Rue Lamartine to the Commissariat of Passy
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rue Lamartine and the Conservatory

stops.name: Paris, rue Lamartine, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; 18 October 1859 is given by Wikipedia, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the Collège de France biography alike. The coordinate is the rue Lamartine in the 9th arrondissement, the street the sources name; the house number is not given anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: In the ninth arrondissement, on the rue Lamartine, a son is born to Michał Bergson, a Warsaw-descended Jewish composer and pianist, and to Katherine Levison, an Englishwoman of a Jewish family from Yorkshire. They name him Henri-Louis. The house has Polish in it, and English, and the French the boy will end by writing. Paris in October 1859 is three years into Haussmann's demolitions. The family is comfortable, on the strength of concerts and of a name that still means something in the salons.
suggested_refs: The rue Lamartine, Paris 9e, Bergson's birth street
sources: Collège de France, official biography of the chair of modern philosophy

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatory and the boy's first schooling
stops.date_confidence: the 1863 move is attested via Wikipedia's articles on Henri and on Michał Bergson; month and day are unknown and default to 01. Coordinate corrected to the Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, 5 place Neuve, per Nominatim (46.2008666, 6.1425027); an earlier working value in the research pool was some 330 metres off.
stops.campa: Michał Bergson takes a post at the Conservatory of Geneva and moves the household to the lake. Henri is four. He begins his schooling in a French-speaking city of watchmakers and Calvinist schoolrooms, small enough that a musician's family is known within a season. The post does not hold. Within a few years the father's career has failed here as it will fail in other cities, and the family begins the drift that will end with its members in three countries at once. Henri is not yet nine when the arrangement that keeps him in France is made.
suggested_refs: Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, place Neuve
Louis M. Greenberg, 'Bergson and Durkheim as Sons and Assimilators: The Early Years' (1976)
sources: Research dossier citing Greenberg (1976), not independently fetched

stops.name: Lycée Fontanes, Paris, the scholarship and the family that leaves
stops.date_confidence: the 1868 enrolment and the stay through 1878 are attested by Wikipedia and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from jean_paul_sartre.journey.json, which already pins the Lycée Condorcet at 48.879, 2.328; Nominatim gives 48.8748, 2.3276 for the modern building, and the research pool reported 48.8776, 2.3283. The three do not agree and the corpus value is kept so the pins coincide.
stops.campa: A scholarship, secured with the help of Geneva's chief rabbi Joseph Wertheimer, boards him in Paris while the rest of the family moves on to London. He enters the Lycée Fontanes, which the Republic will shortly rename Condorcet, and stays ten years, a boarder among day boys with his parents across the Channel. The school becomes the fixed thing. His masters begin to argue among themselves about which subject the boy belongs to: he has taken the first prize in rhetoric, then the first prize in philosophy, then the first prize in mathematics, one after another.
suggested_refs: Lycée Condorcet, Paris 9e, formerly Lycée Bonaparte and Lycée Fontanes

stops.name: Paris, the mathematics prize in the Concours général
stops.date_confidence: the 1877 mathematics prize and the 1878 printing of his solution in the Nouvelles annales de mathématiques are attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and by the journal issue itself (NAM 1878, ser. 2 vol. 17, p. 268). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The teacher's remark about a mere philosopher is tradition, not document. Coordinate is the Sorbonne quarter, the Concours général's Paris venue; the actual hall is not named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: He wins the mathematics prize in the Concours général with a solution the Nouvelles annales de mathématiques prints the following year over a schoolboy's name. His mathematics master, told that the boy has chosen philosophy, is said to have answered that he could have been a mathematician and will now be a mere philosopher. The remark is in every life of him and traces to no document. The man who will spend forty years arguing that intelligence is a tool built for handling solids was, at seventeen, extremely good at handling them. The solution is printed on page 268.
suggested_refs: Nouvelles annales de mathématiques, 1878, ser. 2 vol. 17, p. 268, Bergson's prize solution
sources: Nouvelles annales de mathématiques (1878), via numdam.org

segments.name: Rue d'Ulm and the Provincial Lycées

stops.name: École normale supérieure, rue d'Ulm, the promotion of 1878
stops.date_confidence: the 1878 entry is attested (SEP, Collège de France). October is the school year's opening and is an ordering convention, not a documented date. CONTRADICTION KEPT OPEN: SEP writes that he was accepted alongside Jean Jaurès and Émile Durkheim, but Wikipedia's Durkheim article says Durkheim entered in 1879 on his third attempt; the compression is SEP's. Naturalization as a French citizen is attested but no source reachable gives its year.
stops.campa: He is admitted to the École normale supérieure on the rue d'Ulm in the promotion of 1878, the same year as Jean Jaurès; Émile Durkheim comes up behind them, on his third attempt. A few dozen men in a small school on a small street will divide French thought between them for the next half century. Bergson reads Herbert Spencer with enthusiasm and then reads him against himself, hunting the place where the evolutionary system gives way, and finds it in what Spencer does with time. Jules Lachelier and Félix Ravaisson are the masters he claims. In 1881 he places second in the agrégation de philosophie.
suggested_refs: École normale supérieure, 45 rue d'Ulm, Paris 5e

stops.name: Angers, the first post
stops.date_confidence: attested as to 1881 and Angers (SEP, Wikipedia, Collège de France biography). October is the school year's opening, used to order the segment; no month is recorded.
stops.campa: His first posting sends him to the lycée at Angers, on the Maine, with additional lectures at the local École supérieure de jeunes filles. He is twenty-two, ranked second in France in his examination, and he teaches the standard course to provincial schoolboys. Two years pass. Nothing in the record of Angers announces anything: he reads, he teaches, he is moved on. The Republic shifts its philosophy masters from town to town like garrison officers. The next posting is the Auvergne.
suggested_refs: Lycée d'Angers and the École supérieure de jeunes filles, Bergson's first teaching posts

stops.name: Clermont-Ferrand, Lucretius and the hypnotized subject
stops.date_confidence: the Clermont-Ferrand years, 1883 to 1888, are attested (Wikipedia, SEP), as is the 1886 article 'De la simulation inconsciente dans l'état d'hypnotisme'. October 1883 orders the segment; no month is recorded. The five-year span here absorbs the 1886 article, which has no separate stop.
stops.campa: Five years at the Lycée Blaise-Pascal under the black volcanic stone of Clermont-Ferrand, with lectures at the university faculty added on top. He edits Lucretius for schools, on atoms falling through the void. He reads the physicians and the new psychologists, and in 1886 publishes an article on unconscious simulation in states of hypnosis: subjects reading, without knowing they are reading, what the operator's own face has already told them. The thesis that will make his name is being assembled here, in the provinces, around the question of what a measured second leaves out.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, 'De la simulation inconsciente dans l'état d'hypnotisme', Revue philosophique de la France et de l'étranger (1886)
Bergson's school edition of Lucretius, Extraits de Lucrèce (1884)

segments.name: The Two Theses and the Return to Paris

stops.name: Collège Rollin, Paris, the return to the city
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTED FROM THE POOL: English Wikipedia says he settled in Paris in 1888, and SEP dates the submission of the two theses to 1888, so the Rollin post begins a year earlier than the pool's chronology had it. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to the Collège Rollin, today's Lycée Jacques-Decour, 12 avenue Trudaine, Paris 9e, per Nominatim (48.88196, 2.3433379); the pool's earlier value fell 750 metres away in the 18th.
stops.campa: He settles in Paris in 1888 and teaches at the Collège Rollin on the avenue Trudaine, a few streets from the ones he was schooled in. He is twenty-eight and the two theses are already written and lodged. Seven years of provincial postings end here. The Rollin year itself is short, and is remembered chiefly because it is the address he holds when the doctorate is conferred. Later he will leave the city only to lecture and, twice, on a government's errand. He never holds a post outside Paris again.
suggested_refs: Lycée Jacques-Decour, 12 avenue Trudaine, formerly the Collège Rollin

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the defense of the two theses
stops.date_confidence: the 1889 defense of both theses is attested (IEP, SEP). The exact day of the soutenance is not given in any reachable source and defaults to 01-01. Coordinate is the Sorbonne, where Paris doctorates in letters were defended.
stops.campa: He defends two theses in one session, as the doctorate then required: the principal one in French, Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience, and a Latin supplement, Quid Aristoteles de loco senserit, on what Aristotle held about place. The Essai argues that the time psychology measures is space in disguise, a row of instants laid side by side, and that duration as it is lived has no instants in it and cannot be counted. Félix Alcan publishes it the same year. English readers will meet it twenty-one years later, retitled Time and Free Will.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience (Alcan, 1889)
Henri Bergson, Quid Aristoteles de loco senserit (1889)

stops.name: Lycée Henri-IV, eight years behind the Panthéon
stops.date_confidence: the appointment shortly after 1889 and the eight-year stay are attested by English Wikipedia ('where he remained for eight years'); the exact start is not dated in any reachable source and 1890-01-01 orders the segment. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Lycée Henri IV, rue Clovis, Paris 5e (48.8461796, 2.3486258); the pool's value sat 160 metres away on the wrong side of the block.
stops.campa: He is appointed to the Lycée Henri-IV, behind the Panthéon on the rue Clovis, and stays eight years. He is thirty when he goes in and thirty-eight when he comes out. He teaches the ordinary programme, corrects the ordinary exercises, and writes Matière et mémoire in the hours around them. The book will get him out of the schools for good. Among the boys who pass through the classroom is Alfred Jarry; Maurice Halbwachs comes later, and will build a sociology out of collective memory.
suggested_refs: Lycée Henri-IV, 23 rue Clovis, Paris 5e

stops.name: Paris, the marriage witnessed by Proust
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION KEPT OPEN: English-language sources including Wikipedia give the wedding as 1891; the French chronology built on the civil register gives 7 January 1892, and the later date is used here as primary without the earlier being dismissed. Proust as witness is attested by Wikipedia. The coordinate is a central-Paris registry pin; the actual mairie is not named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: He marries Louise Neuburger, of a Jewish family of the Paris haute bourgeoisie. Her young cousin Marcel Proust, twenty years old and the author of nothing yet, signs as witness, and from that afternoon the philosopher of duration and the novelist of recovered time are cousins by marriage. The household Louise makes is quiet, closed, and unhelpful to journalists. She will be the one who reports, after his death, what he said in private about conversion and about staying where he was.
suggested_refs: Soulez and Worms, Bergson: biographie
Marcel Proust's signature as witness at the Bergson-Neuburger wedding
sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Henri Bergson' (7 January 1892)

stops.name: Paris, the sixteenth arrondissement, the birth of Jeanne
stops.date_confidence: 16 March 1893 in the 16th arrondissement is given by French Wikipedia and independently by the Musée Bourdelle students' directory (16/03/1893); some English summaries give 1896 and that discrepancy is not resolved here. The address in 1893 is unknown: the coordinate is the family's later house at 47 boulevard de Beauséjour, in the right arrondissement, and is therefore approximate as to the birth itself.
stops.campa: Their only child is born in the sixteenth arrondissement on the sixteenth of March 1893 and named Jeanne Adèle. She is deaf. She will be taught to draw and to model, will train under the sculptor Antoine Bourdelle, and will spend her working life as an artist inside a household organized around a father who wrote that the deepest thing in a life is a continuity no language cuts into pieces. There is no second child. After his death she keeps his study exactly as it stood.
suggested_refs: Musée Bourdelle, directory of Bourdelle's students, entry for Jeanne Bergson
The Bergson study and papers at the Bibliothèque littéraire Jacques Doucet

stops.name: Paris, Matter and Memory and the cone
stops.date_confidence: 1896 publication is attested (IEP, Collège de France). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The stop is anchored at the Lycée Henri-IV, where Bergson was teaching when the book appeared, rather than at the publisher's address; the pool's publisher coordinate was not Félix Alcan's house in any case (Alcan was at 108 boulevard Saint-Germain, roughly 48.8524, 2.3406).
stops.campa: Matière et mémoire comes out with Félix Alcan while he is still a lycée master. The brain, it argues, does not store memories at all; it selects and it enacts, a switchboard turned toward action, and the past survives whole without needing any physical place to be kept in. It is the work that opens the Collège de France to him. The book carries the diagram of the cone, its point resting on the plane of the present, the entire mass of a life narrowing into the act of this instant.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire (Alcan, 1896)
Matter and Memory, trans. N. M. Paul and W. S. Palmer (Macmillan 1912; Zone Books 1990; Dover 2004)

segments.name: The Collège de France and the Boom

stops.name: Collège de France, the chair that was not the one he wanted
stops.date_confidence: 1900 entry to the Collège de France in the chair of Greek and Latin philosophy, succeeding Charles Lévêque after losing the modern philosophy chair to Gabriel Tarde, is attested (Wikipedia, Collège de France). Month unknown, defaulted to 01. The 1898 maître de conférences and professorship at the ENS, also attested, are folded into this stop rather than given one of their own. Coordinate inherited as the canonical corpus pin for the Collège de France, as reported by the interlock lens from georges_sorel.journey.json and victoria_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: After two years back on the rue d'Ulm as maître de conférences and then professor, he stands for the chair of modern philosophy at the Collège de France and loses it to Gabriel Tarde. He enters the house anyway, by the chair of Greek and Latin philosophy, succeeding Charles Lévêque. The Collège enrols no students and confers no degrees; its professors lecture to whoever comes in off the place Marcelin-Berthelot and sits down. Anyone may come. Within a few years the room will not hold the people who do.
suggested_refs: Collège de France, 11 place Marcelin-Berthelot, Paris 5e
sources: Collège de France, official biography of the chair of modern philosophy

stops.name: Paris, Laughter and the mechanical in the living
stops.date_confidence: 1900 publication of Le Rire, gathering essays first printed in the Revue de Paris, is attested (Wikipedia, IEP). Month unknown; June orders it after the Collège de France appointment in the same year. The stop sits at his new lecture pin rather than at a publisher's address.
stops.campa: Le Rire gathers three essays from the Revue de Paris into a book about what makes a body funny. The answer is rigidity. The comic shows wherever something mechanical is visible through something living: the man who goes on walking after the street has turned, the gesture repeated once too often, the official who has become his own function. Laughter is a social corrective, aimed by a group at whoever has stopped adapting. He is writing about comedy and about the whole of his philosophy at once, approaching it from the side where it is easiest to laugh.
stops.quote: Something mechanical encrusted upon the living, will represent a cross at which we must halt, a central image from which the imagination branches off in different directions.
stops.quote_source: Henri Bergson, Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of the Comic, trans. Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell (1911), chapter I; verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 4352
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, Le Rire: Essai sur la signification du comique (1900)
Laughter, trans. Brereton and Rothwell (1911), Project Gutenberg 4352

stops.name: Institut de France, the Académie des sciences morales et politiques
stops.date_confidence: election in 1901 is attested (Wikipedia, IEP). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Institut de France on the quai Conti, accurate to within about 80 metres.
stops.campa: He is elected to the Académie des sciences morales et politiques and takes a seat under the dome on the quai Conti. It is the first of the institutional honors and it places him inside the Third Republic's own apparatus of learning: the Institut, the Collège, the reviews, the juries. Thirteen years on he will preside over this body himself. He is forty-two. Nothing he has published is easy and none of it is written for specialists. What carries him into a room of elected notables is the prose.
suggested_refs: Académie des sciences morales et politiques, Institut de France, quai Conti

stops.name: Collège de France, Tarde's chair and the method of intuition
stops.date_confidence: succession to Gabriel Tarde in the chair of modern philosophy in 1904 is attested (Wikipedia, Collège de France); month unknown, defaulted to 01. The 1903 publication of 'Introduction à la métaphysique' in the Revue de métaphysique et de morale is attested by SEP and folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: Gabriel Tarde dies and Bergson moves into the chair of modern philosophy, the post refused him four years before. The year previous, the Revue de métaphysique et de morale had printed his Introduction à la métaphysique, the shortest statement of his method he ever wrote: analysis walks around an object and translates it into symbols, always from a point of view and always in a language; intuition enters the object and coincides with whatever is singular in it and therefore cannot be said. Two ways of knowing, and the second one has no words of its own.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, 'Introduction à la métaphysique', Revue de métaphysique et de morale (1903)

stops.name: Collège de France, Creative Evolution
stops.date_confidence: 1907 publication of L'Évolution créatrice, and the term élan vital with it, are attested (Wikipedia, IEP). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Anchored at his lecture pin, where the material was taught, rather than at the publisher's address.
stops.campa: L'Évolution créatrice appears and turns a professor into a public figure. Life is not a mechanism unfolding a plan already written, and it is not a design executed from outside; it is an impulse, the élan vital, driving through matter and dividing as it goes, into the instinct of the insect and the intelligence of the man, each of them blind in exactly the region where the other sees. Biologists read it, and novelists, and clergy, and a great many people who read no other philosophy. Within four years it is in English and Oxford has invited him over.
stops.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
stops.quote_source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911), chapter I; verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 26163
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, L'Évolution créatrice (Alcan, 1907)
Creative Evolution, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911), Project Gutenberg 26163

stops.name: Collège de France, the crowd and the snobinettes
stops.date_confidence: the phenomenon runs roughly 1907 to 1914 and is attested by Emily Herring's research on Bergson's public and by contemporary press caricature of his audience; 1909 is a midpoint chosen to order the segment, not a documented year. Sorel's attendance is attested by English and French Wikipedia but undated; NOTE, georges_sorel.journey.json places his attendance at the Collège de France in 1893, when Bergson was still at the Lycée Henri-IV and had not yet entered the Collège. Ocampo's attendance is dated 1906 in her own file.
stops.campa: The lectures become an event. Rooms fill an hour before he arrives; carriages block the rue des Écoles; diplomats, society women, journalists and the merely curious take the benches philosophy students had counted on. The press names the audience bergsoniennes and snobinettes, and treats a crowded room as proof that the thought inside it must be soft. Georges Sorel, out of the provinces and out of the engineering service, takes from these lectures the conviction that a revolution is undergone and not calculated. Victoria Ocampo, sixteen and half-clandestine, sat here and said afterward that the account of duration marked her for life.
stops.quote: The universe endures. The more we study the nature of time, the more we shall comprehend that duration means invention, the creation of forms, the continual elaboration of the absolutely new.
stops.quote_source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911), chapter I; verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 26163
suggested_refs: Emily Herring, 'Henri Bergson: the philosopher damned for his female fans', Aeon
Emily Herring, Herald of a Restless World (2024)
sources: Emily Herring, Aeon essay on Bergson's audiences

segments.name: The English Season and the American Crowd

stops.name: Oxford, The Perception of Change
stops.date_confidence: the Oxford lectures and the honorary doctorate of science are attested (Wikipedia, Collège de France, SEP). The lectures were delivered in May 1911 according to the standard bibliography; the day is not given and defaults to 01. Coordinate is the Sheldonian Theatre and the central university buildings.
stops.campa: He lectures at Oxford on the perception of change: that we take movement as a series of stills and then set ourselves the problem of putting the movement back into them, when the change was what was given first and the stills are our own manufacture. Philosophy's difficulties, he tells them, are made this way and can be unmade the same way. He is fifty-one, and this is the country where his mother was born and where his father died. The university makes him an honorary doctor of science.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, La Perception du changement, two lectures at Oxford (1911)

stops.name: Birmingham, the Huxley Lecture
stops.date_confidence: the Huxley Lecture at Birmingham on 'Life and Consciousness' in 1911 is attested by Wikipedia and general Bergson bibliography; no month is given in any reachable source, and June is used only to order it after the Oxford lectures of the same English season. Coordinate is the University of Birmingham Great Hall at Edgbaston.
stops.campa: At Birmingham he gives the Huxley Lecture, endowed in the name of the man who spent his career defending Darwin, and speaks on life and consciousness. Consciousness, he tells the hall, extends exactly as far as choice extends, and shrinks toward zero wherever action has become automatic; a habit perfectly acquired is a piece of unconscious matter again. An audience raised on Huxley's mechanism is being handed a life that is not a mechanism, in a lecture named for the mechanist. Nobody wrote down how they took it.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, 'Life and Consciousness', the Huxley Lecture, University of Birmingham (1911)

stops.name: London, four lectures on the nature of the soul
stops.date_confidence: the four University of London lectures on 'The Nature of the Soul' in 1911 are attested (Wikipedia, Collège de France); no month is recorded and October orders them after Oxford. CORRECTED COORDINATE: the pool pinned Bloomsbury and Senate House, which the university did not occupy until 1937. In 1911 the University of London was housed at the Imperial Institute building in South Kensington, and this coordinate is that site; the specific lecture hall is not named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Four lectures at the University of London on the nature of the soul, in a single English season that also takes in Oxford and Birmingham. The subject is survival: whether consciousness overflows the brain sufficiently that its persistence after the brain becomes a question for evidence and not only for faith. A professor of the Collège de France is arguing, in careful French, before an English audience, that the immortality of the soul is an empirical problem and should be handed to people who collect data. Two years later the Society for Psychical Research elects him president.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, 'The Nature of the Soul', four lectures, University of London (1911)

stops.name: Columbia University, New York, the crowd on Morningside Heights
stops.date_confidence: the February 1913 visit at Columbia's invitation, the lectures, and the Columbia librarians' bibliography with an introduction by John Dewey are attested (SEP, Columbia records via the dossier). The day is not given and defaults to 01. The claim that the crowd produced the first traffic jam in New York's history is [R]: 1914-1918-online asserts it flatly and without evidence, English Wikipedia does not mention it at all, and no source establishes the superlative.
stops.campa: He crosses to New York on Columbia's invitation and lectures on spirituality and liberty and on his own method. The librarians have prepared him a welcome gift, a bibliography of everything he has written, with an introduction by John Dewey. He is fifty-three. The crowd on Morningside Heights is larger than any crowd a philosopher has drawn in the city, and it is from this week that the story dates of New York's first traffic jam, caused by a Frenchman talking about time.
stops.quote: Our intellect, in the narrow sense of the word, is intended to secure the perfect fitting of our body to its environment, to represent the relations of external things among themselves, in short, to think matter.
stops.quote_source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911), introduction; verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 26163 (a comma stands where the original has a dash)
suggested_refs: Columbia University Libraries, bibliography of Bergson with an introduction by John Dewey (1913)

stops.name: London, the Society for Psychical Research
stops.date_confidence: the presidency, taken in May 1913, is attested by Wikipedia; the presidential address 'Fantômes de vivants et recherche psychique' is [R], resting on SPR records as relayed through the psi-encyclopedia and the dossier rather than on a page independently fetched. The day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He accepts the presidency of the Society for Psychical Research and addresses it on phantasms of the living. The interest is not credulity and it is not conversion. It follows straight out of Matière et mémoire, where the brain narrows and filters a consciousness wider than itself. If the filter is what limits us, then the reports of people who seem to see at a distance are data about the filter, and the Society is where such data are gathered. He gives the address in French to a room that has spent thirty years arguing about mediums.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, 'Fantômes de vivants et recherche psychique', presidential address to the Society for Psychical Research (1913)
psi-encyclopedia.spr.ac.uk, 'Henri Bergson'
sources: SPR records via psi-encyclopedia.spr.ac.uk (not independently fetched)

stops.name: Edinburgh, the Gifford Lectures that were never finished
stops.date_confidence: attested that Bergson gave Giffords at Edinburgh on 'The Problem of Personality' and that the war stopped the planned continuation (Wikipedia, SEP). The Gifford archives date the series to 1913-14 and give no month and no lecture count: the figure of eleven lectures and the date May 1914 rest on the research dossier alone and are [R]. Coordinate corrected to Old College, roughly 55.9479, -3.1866.
stops.campa: The Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh, on the problem of personality, with a second series promised for the following year. The war cancels the second series. The text is never published, and in the 1930s he writes a will instructing that all his papers be destroyed; the instruction is carried out. What was said in Old College survives only in listeners' notes and in the archive's bare title. What he had worked out about personality, and what the second series would have argued, nobody now knows.
suggested_refs: Gifford Lectures archive, 'The Problem of Personality', Edinburgh 1913-14
Bergson's testamentary instruction that his papers be destroyed

segments.name: The War: the Academy, the Index, the Missions

stops.name: Institut de France, elected to the Académie française
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Académie française's own records: elected 12 February 1914 to the seat of Émile Ollivier.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of February the Académie française elects him to the seat of Émile Ollivier, the minister who took France into the war of 1870 and spent the forty years after it explaining himself in print. The reception, with its sword and its green-embroidered coat and its obligatory eulogy of the predecessor, is scheduled and then postponed. The war intervenes, and it will be four years before he stands under the dome. Three and a half months after the election, Rome condemns his books.
suggested_refs: Académie française, seat 11, formerly Émile Ollivier's

stops.name: Paris, the books placed on the Index
stops.date_confidence: the placing of Bergson's major works on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum on 1 June 1914 is attested (SEP, cross-checked against the dossier's citation of Bruno Neveu, 'Bergson et l'Index'). The stop sits at Bergson's own canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identical from the corpus, rather than at the Vatican: the decree was issued in Rome by a body he never appeared before, and a stop belongs to whoever was there.
stops.campa: On the first of June the Congregation of the Index places his major works among the books Catholics may not read. The Modernist crisis is at its height, and his evolution, his intuition, and his God who is not a first cause of the scholastic sort have been read in Rome as a philosophy for priests looking for a way out. He is in Paris. The decree reaches him as a printed line in a list. Twenty-three years later he will write in his own will that his thinking had been carrying him toward that Church the whole time.
suggested_refs: Bruno Neveu, 'Bergson et l'Index'
Decree of the Congregation of the Index, 1 June 1914

stops.name: Institut de France, the meaning of the war
stops.date_confidence: the presidential address 'La signification de la guerre' to the Académie des sciences morales et politiques in December 1914 is attested by English Wikipedia; the day is not given and defaults to 01. The article 'La force qui s'use et celle qui ne s'use pas', published in the Bulletin des Armées de la République on 4 November 1914, is attested to the day and is folded into this stop rather than given its own. NOTE: the research pool had a separate August 1914 address at the same body, which no reachable source supports and which appears to conflate these two utterances.
stops.campa: As president of the Académie des sciences morales et politiques he delivers an address on the meaning of the war, five months into it. In November he has already put an article in the Bulletin des Armées on the force that wears itself out and the force that does not. The argument is his own philosophy conscripted: Germany as mechanism, mass, and calculated force, which depletes as it is spent; France and her allies as moral energy, which does not. The élan vital has been enlisted. It appears in English as The Meaning of the War.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, La signification de la guerre (1915), in English as The Meaning of the War
Bulletin des Armées de la République, 4 November 1914
sources: Écrits et paroles, collected wartime addresses

stops.name: Madrid, the Ateneo and the king
stops.date_confidence: the 1916 Spanish mission, the appearance at the Ateneo de Madrid and the meeting with Alfonso XIII rest on a contemporaneous memoir cited in the research dossier and on a Cambridge Core chapter about the Casa de Velázquez; no month is given and defaults to 01. Tagged as attested but on a single documentary line, not on multiple independent sources.
stops.campa: France sends him to Madrid, into a neutral kingdom whose elites are being courted hard by both belligerents. He appears at the Ateneo and is received by Alfonso XIII. The mission is cultural in form and political in substance: a philosopher whose books are already read in Spanish drawing rooms is himself the argument for the civilization he says is being defended. He is fifty-six, and this is his first crossing of the Pyrenees on a government's account. Spain stays neutral to the end of the war.
suggested_refs: Ateneo de Madrid
Casa de Velázquez, founded in the aftermath of these French cultural missions

stops.name: The White House, Washington, the philosopher sent to Wilson
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTED FROM THE POOL: 1914-1918-online states that in January 1917 the French government sent Bergson to the United States as a special envoy to meet Wilson, i.e. before American entry, which was the point of the trip. The pool had framed him as travelling with the Viviani mission, which in fact visited in April and May 1917, after entry, when Bergson was already in the country. English Wikipedia says nothing about a Wilson meeting; the meeting rests on 1914-1918-online and on Geert Somsen's 2020 article. Day unknown, defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In January the French government sends him to Washington as a special envoy, bilingual through his English mother, to put the case for American entry to the president himself. He meets Woodrow Wilson and raises with him the shape of a league of nations for afterward. In April the United States declares war, and in the spring the official French mission under René Viviani arrives to find Bergson already there. Whether a philosopher moved a president is not a question the archives answer, and Bergson never claimed it in print.
suggested_refs: Geert Somsen, 'The Philosopher and the Rooster: Henri Bergson's French Diplomatic Missions, 1914-1925' (2020)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henri Bergson' (for the Viviani mission dates)

stops.name: Institut de France, received under the dome
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Académie française: received 24 January 1918, with René Doumic delivering the response.
stops.campa: Four years after the election he is received into the Académie française on the quai Conti, and René Doumic answers his speech. The seat is Ollivier's, and the eulogy of a predecessor is the form the ceremony takes, so Bergson praises a man whose name had become a byword for the catastrophe of 1870 while a larger catastrophe is being fought out ninety kilometres from the room. He is fifty-eight, the son of a Warsaw musician and an Englishwoman, and he wears the uniform of the Republic, the sword, the embroidered palms. Paris is under long-range shelling that winter.
suggested_refs: Académie française, discours de réception de Henri Bergson, 24 January 1918, with the response by René Doumic

stops.name: Washington, the second American stay
stops.date_confidence: 1914-1918-online confirms a protracted second stay from May to September 1918. CORRECTED FROM THE POOL: this stay was not attached to the Viviani mission, which was a discrete visit in April and May 1917; the Viviani preface Bergson wrote belongs to the earlier trip. Day unknown, defaults to 01. Coordinate is the French embassy quarter of Washington and is approximate.
stops.campa: He returns to the United States from May to September for a longer stay, this one inside the machinery of Allied cooperation and postwar planning rather than persuasion. The country is a belligerent now and the argument he was sent to make in 1917 has already been won by events; what is left is committees, memoranda, and the shape of the peace. His hands have begun to stiffen; in a few years they will not manage a signature. He does not cross an ocean again.
suggested_refs: Bergson's preface to René Viviani, La Mission française en Amérique (1917), belonging to the earlier trip

stops.name: Cambridge, the doctorate and the end of the lecturing
stops.date_confidence: the Cambridge honorary doctorate in June 1920, and the Collège de France relieving him of teaching duties around the same period, are attested by English Wikipedia; the day is not given and defaults to 01. Coordinate is the Senate House at Cambridge, where honorary degrees are conferred; no source names the venue and the pin is inferred.
stops.campa: Cambridge confers an honorary doctorate. In the same season the Collège de France relieves him of the duty of lecturing, appointing a deputy and leaving him the chair; the arthritis has begun, and the crowds that made his name have become physically impossible to face. From here the work is done sitting down, in a house in the sixteenth arrondissement, with a secretary and a correspondence. He is sixty. The public performance is finished; the life has twenty years left to run.
suggested_refs: University of Cambridge, honorary doctorate conferred June 1920

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the session with Einstein
stops.date_confidence: the Société française de philosophie session on relativity during Einstein's Paris visit, with Langevin, Hadamard, Cartan and Painlevé present, is attested; SEP discusses the dispute in general terms. The exact date of 6 April 1922 comes from the Société's session records via the research dossier and Jimena Canales's book, and was not independently re-verified.
stops.campa: During Einstein's visit to Paris the Société française de philosophie holds a session on relativity with Einstein in the room. Langevin is there, and Hadamard, Cartan, Painlevé. Bergson accepts the physics and disputes the extrapolation: the multiple times of the theory are ways of measuring, and underneath every measurement there is one duration, lived and undivided, which no clock reaches. Einstein answers that there is no philosophers' time, that there is the time of psychology and the time of physics and nothing else. Neither man moves.
suggested_refs: Jimena Canales, The Physicist and the Philosopher (2015)
Bulletin de la Société française de philosophie, session of 6 April 1922
sources: Société française de philosophie session records via sofrphilo.fr (dossier)

stops.name: Paris, Duration and Simultaneity
stops.date_confidence: 1922 publication is attested (Wikipedia); no month is recorded, and June is used to order the book after the April session it answers. Coordinate is Félix Alcan's house at 108 boulevard Saint-Germain; the research pool carried a publisher coordinate that was not Alcan's address at all and it is corrected here.
stops.campa: Durée et simultanéité comes out in the same year, an attempt to draw a border: relativity is right about clocks and wrong the moment it is extended into a metaphysics of time. Physicists take it apart, and a number of the objections are technical and land. He stops promoting the book, drops it from the list of his works, and leaves it out of the collected editions prepared in his lifetime. In a letter of 1924 he is still calling relativity a very great advance.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, Durée et simultanéité: à propos de la théorie d'Einstein (1922), archive.org

stops.name: Palais Wilson, Geneva, the first chair of intellectual cooperation
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTED FROM THE POOL: Wikipedia's ICIC article gives formal establishment in August 1922, a first session on 1 August 1922, Bergson as inaugural chair presiding 1922 to 1925, and the Palais Wilson as the seat between 1922 and 1937. The 1920-1925 span carried in some summaries is simply wrong, since the committee did not exist in 1920, and is not preserved here as a live discrepancy. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Palais Wilson, 51 quai Wilson (46.2148896, 6.1510578).
stops.campa: The League of Nations sets up an International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation and Bergson takes the chair at its first session, in the Palais Wilson on the Geneva lakefront. Albert Einstein sits on the committee, three months after the argument in the Sorbonne, and so does Marie Curie. The work is to rebuild scholarly exchange across borders that four years of war have shut. The committee has no money and no power to compel anybody to do anything. He presides until 1925. It is the body Unesco is eventually built out of.
suggested_refs: Palais Wilson, 51 quai Wilson, Geneva, seat of the League of Nations and of the ICIC 1922-1937
UN Geneva library, International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation, notable members

stops.name: Paris, the hands that will not close
stops.date_confidence: severe rheumatoid arthritis from the mid-1920s onward, with repeated unsuccessful treatments including clinics and thermal spas, is attested by Marcel-Francis Kahn's medical-historical study. No individual clinic or spa is named in any reachable source and no year is fixed for the onset: 1925 orders the segment. The coordinate is his own house in the 16th arrondissement, not any spa, because the spas cannot be located.
stops.campa: Rheumatoid arthritis takes his hands and then his walking. He goes to clinics and to thermal spas, repeatedly, and none of the treatments does anything at all. The public life closes: no more lectures, no more crossings, few visitors admitted. He dictates, and is read to, and is carried. He had written that the whole of the past is preserved and presses forward into the present; the body it presses into can no longer act. He goes on working for another nine years.
stops.quote: To exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.
stops.quote_source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911), chapter I; verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 26163
suggested_refs: Marcel-Francis Kahn, medical-historical study of Bergson's rheumatoid arthritis (PubMed 20729121)

stops.name: Paris, the Nobel Prize collected in absence
stops.date_confidence: Bergson is the designated laureate for 1927, but the 1927 literature prize was reserved and actually conferred in 1928, which is why IEP writes that he received it in 1928; both years are right about different things. The ceremony date is not verified here and the date defaults to 1928-01-01. nobelprize.org returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, so the citation text rests on Wikipedia's quotation of the Nobel Foundation. The stop sits at Bergson's own house and not in Stockholm, because illness kept him from travelling and he was never there.
stops.campa: The Swedish Academy gives him the Nobel Prize in Literature, in recognition of his rich and vitalizing ideas and the brilliant skill with which they have been presented, a citation that praises the prose and leaves the argument alone. He is too ill to travel and the ceremony in Stockholm proceeds without him. The prize comes to the sixteenth arrondissement instead, to a man who can no longer stand up. In 1930 France makes him a Grand-Croix of the Legion of Honour, the highest rank it has to give.
suggested_refs: Nobel Foundation, literature prize for 1927, awarded to Henri Bergson
Grand-Croix de la Légion d'honneur, 1930
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henri Bergson', quoting the Nobel Foundation (nobelprize.org itself returned HTTP 403)

stops.name: 47 boulevard de Beauséjour, The Two Sources
stops.date_confidence: 1932 publication of Les Deux Sources de la morale et de la religion is attested (Wikipedia, IEP), as is La Pensée et le mouvant in 1934, which is folded into this stop. Months unknown, defaulted to 01. Anchored at his house rather than at a publisher's address; the coordinate is Nominatim's 47 boulevard de Beauséjour (48.8569653, 2.2680222), which corrects a value in the research pool that sat 230 metres off.
stops.campa: After seventeen years without a book he publishes Les Deux Sources de la morale et de la religion. There are two moralities and not one: the closed morality of the group, which is pressure and defends a tribe against the tribe next to it, and the open morality, which is aspiration and stops at no boundary. And two religions: the static one, which manufactures myths against the knowledge of death, and the dynamic one of the mystics, whom he treats not as poets but as witnesses producing evidence. La Pensée et le mouvant follows two years later and closes the published work.
suggested_refs: Henri Bergson, Les Deux Sources de la morale et de la religion (1932)
Henri Bergson, La Pensée et le mouvant (1934)
Gilles Deleuze, Le Bergsonisme (1966), which reopened the reading of these books

stops.name: 47 boulevard de Beauséjour, the testament
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the will is dated 7 February 1937 and English Wikipedia quotes it directly. The quotation used here is the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's contemporary translation, printed 26 September 1941; the awkward English is the JTA translator's and is quoted as printed rather than smoothed.
stops.campa: On the seventh of February he writes his will. His reflections, he sets down, have brought him nearer and nearer to Catholicism, in which he sees the complete fulfillment of Judaism. He would have converted. He does not, and he gives the reason: a wave of anti-Semitism is preparing itself across the world, and he intends to be counted among the people who are going to be persecuted. He asks that a Catholic priest be present at his funeral if the archbishop of Paris permits it. The document stays in the drawer while he is alive.
stops.quote: I would have become converted had I not seen in preparation for many years a formidable wave of anti-Semitism which was sweeping over the world. I decided to remain among those who could be persecuted.
stops.quote_source: Bergson's testament of 7 February 1937, in the translation printed by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Rise of Anti-Semitism Inspired Bergson to Remain a Jew, His Will Reveals', 26 September 1941; two contiguous sentences of the JTA excerpt
suggested_refs: Le Monde archive, 'Le testament de Bergson', 3 June 1954
Jewish Telegraphic Agency archive, 26 September 1941

stops.name: Passy, the commissariat of the sixteenth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: the refusal of exemption is attested by a contemporary JTA report of 9 December 1940. The visit to the local commissariat, and the exact wording said to have been entered on the form, are [R]: transmitted tradition, never produced from the original document. Vichy's Statut des Juifs is dated 3 October 1940 and the exemption clause for exceptional scientific merit belongs to the statute of 18 October, so the registration falls in the autumn; the day is unknown and defaults to 01. The coordinate is the Passy quarter of the 16th arrondissement and is approximate.
stops.campa: Vichy's statute of the third of October requires Jews to declare themselves, and the statute of the eighteenth exempts those of exceptional scientific merit. The exemption is offered to him. He refuses it, gives up his post, and goes to the police station of his own arrondissement to register, carried, his hands long since useless. The words he is said to have written on the form are repeated in every account and have never been produced from the original: Academic. Philosopher. Nobel Prize winner. Jew.
stops.quote: The world famous philosopher, Prof. Henri Bergson, has declined exemption from the anti-Jewish statute of Oct. 18, to which he is entitled under the section making exception for persons of 'exceptional scientific merits.'
stops.quote_source: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Bergson Refuses Exemption Under French Anti-Jewish Law, To Quit College Post', 9 December 1940
suggested_refs: Vichy Statut des Juifs, 3 October 1940, and the statute of 18 October 1940
Jewish Telegraphic Agency archive, 9 December 1940

stops.name: 47 boulevard de Beauséjour, the night of the third
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION KEPT OPEN. 3 January is given by English Wikipedia, French Wikipedia, SEP, and the Académie française's own biographical index page; 4 January is given by IEP, by Paul Valéry's memorial address of 9 January 1941 on the Académie's own site, and by 1914-1918-online. The Académie is internally inconsistent and cannot settle it, so the death falls in the night of 3-4 January 1941 and the file takes the 3rd only as its sortable value. Cause: pulmonary congestion per Valéry, bronchitis per Wikipedia, pneumonia per IEP.
stops.campa: He dies at 47 boulevard de Beauséjour in the night, eighty-one years old, in a city under German occupation. The cause is entered as pulmonary congestion by the Academy, as bronchitis in some accounts and pneumonia in others. The story that he caught the illness standing in a cold queue outside the police station has been in circulation ever since; the Stanford Encyclopedia calls it a rumor, and nothing in the record joins the registration to the death except the shape of the story. On the ninth of January Paul Valéry delivers the Academy's tribute.

stops.name: Garches, the grave west of Paris
stops.date_confidence: burial at the cemetery of Garches is attested (Wikipedia, SEP, French Wikipedia); the day of the funeral is not given in any reachable source and 6 January orders it between the death and Valéry's address of 9 January. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Cimetière de Garches (48.8480054, 2.1938773); a value carried in the research pool fell 1.1 km outside the cemetery.
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of Garches, west of Paris, in a small funeral under occupation conditions, with a Catholic priest saying prayers at his own request and no conversion ever having taken place. His daughter Jeanne leaves his papers to the Bibliothèque littéraire Jacques Doucet. In 1967 a decree of the Republic has his name cut into a pillar of the Panthéon, in the nave, among the inscriptions. He is not moved there. The grave at Garches is where he stays.
stops.quote: I would have converted [to Catholicism], if I had not seen over many years the great wave of anti-semitism preparing itself to expand over the world.
stops.quote_source: Louise Bergson's report of her husband's words, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Henri Bergson'; the bracketed gloss is the encyclopedia's
